The results suggest that genotype-dependent differences in the cisplatin response are predominantly associated with the 6h timepoint, although agreement between pipelines varies substantially.

Across the four pipelines, the joint genotype-interaction test identified 2,209 significant proteins in AlphaDIA, 905 in DIA-NN, 497 in Spectronaut, and 19 in MaxDIA (BH FDR < 0.05). Among 7,460 proteins tested by all four pipelines, only 16 were significant in all four, indicating limited consensus in statistical detection. However, these 16 proteins showed strong agreement in their 6h interaction effect sizes (Pearson r = 0.926–0.993), with consistent effect directions across all pipelines. In contrast, 24h effect-size correlations were weaker (r = −0.182–0.616), and none of the 16 proteins showed an individually significant 24h interaction. Together, these findings support a reproducible early genotype-dependent cisplatin response among a small consensus protein set.

### Within-condition quantitative reproducibility
```{r within-condition-reproducibility}
# Reuse existing QFeatures objects
qf_models <- list(
  AlphaDIA = qf_alpha,
  `DIA-NN` = qf_diann,
  Spectronaut = qf_spectro,
  MaxDIA = qf_maxdia
)

# Extract within-condition, within-batch protein variability
reproducibility_results <- lapply(names(qf_models), function(software) {

  assay <- qf_models[[software]][["proteins"]]
  abund <- SummarizedExperiment::assay(assay)

  # Match sample metadata to abundance matrix columns
  metadata <- design_data[
    match(colnames(abund), design_data$Run),
    c("Run", "condition", "Batch")
  ]

  stopifnot(
    !anyNA(metadata$Run),
    identical(as.character(metadata$Run), colnames(abund))
  )

  groups <- split(
    seq_len(ncol(abund)),
    interaction(metadata$condition, metadata$Batch, drop = TRUE)
  )

  # Retain groups with at least two biological replicates
  groups <- groups[lengths(groups) >= 2]

  bind_rows(lapply(names(groups), function(group_name) {

    idx <- groups[[group_name]]

    x <- abund[, idx, drop = FALSE]

    n_observed <- rowSums(is.finite(x))

    protein_sd <- apply(x, 1, function(z) {
      z <- z[is.finite(z)]
      if (length(z) < 2) return(NA_real_)
      sd(z)
    })

    data.frame(
      Software = software,
      Protein = rownames(abund),
      Condition = as.character(metadata$condition[idx[1]]),
      Batch = as.character(metadata$Batch[idx[1]]),
      N_replicates = length(idx),
      N_observed = n_observed,
      SD_log2 = protein_sd
    )
  }))
}) |>
  bind_rows()

# Summarize within-group variability for each pipeline
reproducibility_summary <- reproducibility_results |>
  filter(is.finite(SD_log2)) |>
  group_by(Software) |>
  summarise(
    Protein_group_measurements = n(),
    Median_SD_log2 = median(SD_log2),
    Q1_SD_log2 = quantile(SD_log2, 0.25),
    Q3_SD_log2 = quantile(SD_log2, 0.75),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

print(reproducibility_summary, n = Inf)

# Compare distributions across pipelines
p_reproducibility <- reproducibility_results |>
  filter(is.finite(SD_log2)) |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = Software,
    y = SD_log2,
    fill = Software
  )) +
  geom_boxplot(
    outlier.shape = NA,
    width = 0.65
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(
    0,
    quantile(
      reproducibility_results$SD_log2[
        is.finite(reproducibility_results$SD_log2)
      ],
      0.95
    )
  )) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = software_colors) +
  labs(
    title = "Within-condition quantitative variability",
    subtitle = "Biological replicates grouped by condition and acquisition batch",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Within-group SD of log2 protein abundance"
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1)
  )

print(p_reproducibility)
```

Within-condition quantitative variability was evaluated using the standard deviation (SD) of log2-transformed protein abundances among biological replicates belonging to the same experimental condition and acquisition batch. DIA-NN exhibited the lowest median within-group SD (0.109), closely followed by AlphaDIA (0.118), whereas Spectronaut showed moderately higher variability (0.145). MaxDIA exhibited the highest median SD (0.261), approximately 2.4-fold greater than DIA-NN. The interquartile ranges followed a similar pattern, with DIA-NN (0.058–0.204) and AlphaDIA (0.064–0.213) displaying narrower variability distributions than Spectronaut (0.075–0.288) and MaxDIA (0.145–0.460). These findings indicate that DIA-NN and AlphaDIA provided the most consistent protein abundance estimates among biological replicates, while MaxDIA showed substantially greater within-condition variability. This observation is consistent with the higher residual variability and lower differential abundance sensitivity previously observed for MaxDIA. However, because the analysis included biological rather than technical replicates and was performed on each pipeline's quantified protein set, these results reflect combined biological and technical variability rather than isolated technical reproducibility.

### 68 Within-condition quantitative reproducibility

Within-condition quantitative variability was assessed using the standard deviation (SD) of log2-transformed protein abundances among biological replicates within the same experimental condition and acquisition batch. DIA-NN exhibited the lowest median SD (0.108), closely followed by AlphaDIA (0.115), whereas Spectronaut showed moderately higher variability (0.144). MaxDIA exhibited the highest median SD (0.266), approximately 2.5-fold greater than DIA-NN. Interquartile ranges showed a similar pattern, with DIA-NN (0.057–0.204) and AlphaDIA (0.062–0.208) displaying narrower variability distributions than Spectronaut (0.074–0.289) and MaxDIA (0.146–0.474). These findings indicate greater within-condition quantitative consistency for DIA-NN and AlphaDIA, whereas MaxDIA showed substantially higher variability. Because the analysis used biological replicates and pipeline-specific protein sets, these estimates reflect combined biological and technical variability rather than isolated technical reproducibility.
Excluding Group 4 did not materially alter the relative reproducibility ranking: DIA-NN ≈ AlphaDIA < Spectronaut < MaxDIA in median within-condition variability.

### Dynamic range and abundance-dependent precision

```{r abundance-dependent-precision, eval=FALSE}
# Restrict to proteins shared by all four pipelines
shared_proteins_precision <- Reduce(
  intersect,
  lapply(qf_models, function(qf) {
    rownames(qf[["proteins"]])
  })
)

abundance_precision <- lapply(names(qf_models), function(software) {

  assay_obj <- qf_models[[software]][["proteins"]]
  idx <- match(shared_proteins_precision, rownames(assay_obj))

  abundance <- SummarizedExperiment::assay(assay_obj)[idx, , drop = FALSE]
  models <- SummarizedExperiment::rowData(assay_obj)$msqrobModels[idx]

  mean_abundance <- rowMeans(abundance, na.rm = TRUE)
  mean_abundance[!is.finite(mean_abundance)] <- NA_real_

  residual_sd <- vapply(models, function(m) {
    if (is.null(m)) return(NA_real_)

    s <- tryCatch(
      methods::slot(m, "params")$sigma,
      error = function(e) NA_real_
    )

    if (length(s) != 1 || !is.finite(s)) NA_real_ else s
  }, numeric(1))

  data.frame(
    Software = software,
    Protein = shared_proteins_precision,
    Mean_log2_abundance = mean_abundance,
    Residual_SD = residual_sd
  )
}) |>
  bind_rows() |>
  filter(
    is.finite(Mean_log2_abundance),
    is.finite(Residual_SD),
    Residual_SD > 0
  ) |>
  group_by(Software) |>
  mutate(
    Abundance_decile = ntile(Mean_log2_abundance, 10)
  ) |>
  ungroup()

# Median residual SD across abundance deciles
abundance_precision_summary <- abundance_precision |>
  group_by(Software, Abundance_decile) |>
  summarise(
    N_proteins = n(),
    Median_residual_SD = median(Residual_SD),
    Q1 = quantile(Residual_SD, 0.25),
    Q3 = quantile(Residual_SD, 0.75),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

print(abundance_precision_summary, n = Inf)

# Summary of low- and high-abundance proteins
abundance_precision_extremes <- abundance_precision_summary |>
  filter(Abundance_decile %in% c(1, 10)) |>
  select(Software, Abundance_decile, Median_residual_SD) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(
    names_from = Abundance_decile,
    values_from = Median_residual_SD,
    names_prefix = "Decile_"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Low_to_high_SD_ratio = Decile_1 / Decile_10
  )

print(abundance_precision_extremes)

# Plot abundance-dependent residual variability
p_abundance_precision <- ggplot(
  abundance_precision_summary,
  aes(
    x = Abundance_decile,
    y = Median_residual_SD,
    color = Software,
    group = Software
  )
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = software_colors) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) +
  labs(
    title = "Abundance-dependent protein quantification precision",
    subtitle = paste(
      length(shared_proteins_precision),
      "shared proteins; abundance deciles defined within each pipeline"
    ),
    x = "Protein abundance decile (low to high)",
    y = "Median model residual SD (log2 scale)",
    color = "DIA pipeline"
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12)

print(p_abundance_precision)
```

Abundance-dependent precision was evaluated across 7,483 proteins shared by all four DIA pipelines by examining fitted residual standard deviations across ten within-pipeline protein abundance deciles. All pipelines generally exhibited decreasing residual variability with increasing protein abundance, although the magnitude of this relationship differed considerably. AlphaDIA and DIA-NN demonstrated consistently low residual SDs across most abundance deciles, decreasing from 0.218 and 0.226 in the lowest decile to 0.138 and 0.120 in the highest decile, respectively. MaxDIA exhibited substantially higher residual variability throughout the abundance range, with median SDs decreasing from 0.435 to 0.296, indicating that its reduced quantitative precision was not restricted to low-abundance proteins. Spectronaut displayed the strongest abundance dependence, with residual SD decreasing from 0.628 in the lowest decile to 0.147 in the highest decile, representing a 4.27-fold difference. Although Spectronaut showed particularly high variability among low-abundance proteins, its precision approached that of AlphaDIA and DIA-NN at higher abundance levels. Overall, these findings indicate that DIA-NN and AlphaDIA maintained comparatively stable quantitative precision across the abundance range, whereas MaxDIA exhibited consistently elevated residual variability and Spectronaut was particularly affected at low abundance.

The pronounced abundance-dependent variability observed for Spectronaut is consistent with the unusual low-intensity distribution identified during initial data quality assessment, when intensity values of exactly 1 were detected and subsequently treated as missing values. Despite this preprocessing correction, Spectronaut retained substantially elevated residual variability among low-abundance proteins, whereas its precision approached that of AlphaDIA and DIA-NN at higher abundance levels. This suggests that low-abundance quantification represents a particular limitation in the processed Spectronaut dataset, although the present analysis cannot establish whether the original intensity-value artifact directly contributed to the remaining variability.

```{r save_temporal_precision_results, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE}
# ============================================================
# SAVE TEMPORAL RESULTS AND MODEL-DEPENDENT SUMMARIES
# No model fitting or hypothesis testing is performed here.
# ============================================================

# 1. Create a separate results directory
results_cache_dir <- file.path(cache_dir, "statistical_results")
dir.create(results_cache_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

# 2. Explicitly named results we want to preserve
priority_objects <- c(
  "temporal_joint_summary",
  "temporal_joint_results",
  "temporal_interaction_summary",
  "temporal_interaction_results",
  "temporal_interaction_agreement",
  "temporal_interaction_effect_agreement",
  "temporal_interaction_time_specific",
  "abundance_precision_summary",
  "abundance_dependent_precision",
  "within_condition_variability"
)

# 3. Find additional relevant objects in the current environment
all_objects <- ls(envir = .GlobalEnv, all.names = TRUE)

additional_objects <- grep(
  "temporal|interaction|precision|residual|msqrob|joint|within_condition",
  all_objects,
  value = TRUE,
  ignore.case = TRUE
)

objects_to_save <- unique(c(priority_objects, additional_objects))
objects_to_save <- intersect(objects_to_save, all_objects)

# 4. Save each available object separately
saved <- character()
failed <- character()

for (nm in objects_to_save) {

  obj <- get(nm, envir = .GlobalEnv, inherits = FALSE)

  # Avoid saving functions, environments, and connections
  if (is.function(obj) || is.environment(obj) ||
      inherits(obj, "connection")) {
    next
  }

  destination <- file.path(
    results_cache_dir,
    paste0(nm, ".rds")
  )

  tryCatch(
    {
      saveRDS(obj, destination, compress = TRUE)
      saved <- c(saved, nm)
      message("Saved: ", nm)
    },
    error = function(e) {
      failed <<- c(failed, nm)
      warning("Could not save ", nm, ": ", conditionMessage(e))
    }
  )
}

# 5. Save a manifest
manifest <- data.frame(
  object_name = saved,
  file_name = paste0(saved, ".rds"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

saveRDS(
  manifest,
  file.path(results_cache_dir, "saved_results_manifest.rds")
)

# 6. Report what was saved
cat("\n====================================\n")
cat("STATISTICAL RESULTS CACHE\n")
cat("====================================\n")
cat("Directory:", results_cache_dir, "\n")
cat("Objects saved:", length(saved), "\n")

if (length(saved) > 0) {
  print(manifest, row.names = FALSE)
} else {
  cat("No matching objects found in the current environment.\n")
}

if (length(failed) > 0) {
  cat("\nObjects that failed to save:\n")
  print(failed)
}
```

### 68 Dynamic range and abundance-dependent precision
```{r abundance_precision_and_save_68, eval=run_analysis, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# ============================================================
# 1. Abundance-dependent precision: 68 retained runs
# ============================================================

software_order_68 <- c("AlphaDIA", "DIA-NN", "Spectronaut", "MaxDIA")

shared_proteins_precision_68 <- Reduce(
  intersect,
  lapply(qf_models_68[software_order_68], function(qf) {
    rownames(qf[["proteins"]])
  })
)

abundance_precision_68 <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  lapply(software_order_68, function(sw) {

    se <- qf_models_68[[sw]][["proteins"]]
    idx <- match(shared_proteins_precision_68, rownames(se))

    abundance <- SummarizedExperiment::assay(se)[idx, , drop = FALSE]
    models <- SummarizedExperiment::rowData(se)[["msqrobModels"]][idx]

    mean_abundance <- rowMeans(abundance, na.rm = TRUE)
    mean_abundance[!is.finite(mean_abundance)] <- NA_real_

    residual_sd <- vapply(models, function(m) {
      if (is.null(m) || !methods::is(m, "StatModel"))
        return(NA_real_)

      s <- m@params$sigma

      if (length(s) != 1L || !is.finite(s) || s <= 0)
        return(NA_real_)

      as.numeric(s)
    }, numeric(1))

    data.frame(
      Software = sw,
      Protein = shared_proteins_precision_68,
      Mean_log2_abundance = mean_abundance,
      Residual_SD = residual_sd
    )
  })
) |>
  dplyr::filter(
    is.finite(Mean_log2_abundance),
    is.finite(Residual_SD),
    Residual_SD > 0
  ) |>
  dplyr::group_by(Software) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    Abundance_decile = dplyr::ntile(Mean_log2_abundance, 10)
  ) |>
  dplyr::ungroup()

# ============================================================
# 2. Summarize residual SD across abundance deciles
# ============================================================

abundance_precision_summary_68 <- abundance_precision_68 |>
  dplyr::group_by(Software, Abundance_decile) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    N_proteins = dplyr::n(),
    Median_residual_SD = median(Residual_SD),
    Q1 = unname(quantile(Residual_SD, 0.25)),
    Q3 = unname(quantile(Residual_SD, 0.75)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

print(abundance_precision_summary_68, n = Inf)

abundance_precision_extremes_68 <- abundance_precision_summary_68 |>
  dplyr::filter(Abundance_decile %in% c(1, 10)) |>
  dplyr::select(
    Software, Abundance_decile, Median_residual_SD
  ) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(
    names_from = Abundance_decile,
    values_from = Median_residual_SD,
    names_prefix = "Decile_"
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    Low_to_high_SD_ratio = Decile_1 / Decile_10
  )

print(abundance_precision_extremes_68)

# ============================================================
# 3. Plot abundance-dependent precision
# ============================================================

p_abundance_precision_68 <- ggplot2::ggplot(
  abundance_precision_summary_68,
  ggplot2::aes(
    x = Abundance_decile,
    y = Median_residual_SD,
    color = Software,
    group = Software
  )
) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 2) +
  ggplot2::scale_color_manual(values = software_colors) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title = "Abundance-dependent protein quantification precision",
    subtitle = paste(
      length(shared_proteins_precision_68),
      "shared proteins; abundance deciles defined within each pipeline"
    ),
    x = "Protein abundance decile (low to high)",
    y = "Median model residual SD\n(log2 scale)",
    color = "DIA pipeline"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_bw(base_size = 12)

print(p_abundance_precision_68)

# ============================================================
# 4. Save 68-run statistical results
# ============================================================

results_cache_dir_68 <- file.path(
  cache_dir, "statistical_results_68"
)

dir.create(
  results_cache_dir_68,
  recursive = TRUE,
  showWarnings = FALSE
)

# Explicitly save important 68-run analysis results
priority_objects_68 <- c(
  "da_results_68",
  "da_summary_68",
  "temporal_joint_summary_68",
  "temporal_joint_results_68",
  "interaction_shared_summary_68",
  "interaction_overlap_summary_68",
  "interaction_consensus_68",
  "interaction_effects_68",
  "interaction_direction_summary_68",
  "interaction_correlations_68",
  "interaction_time_summary_68",
  "interaction_time_pattern_summary_68",
  "reproducibility_summary_68",
  "reproducibility_results_68",
  "abundance_precision_summary_68",
  "abundance_precision_extremes_68",
  "abundance_precision_68"
)

# Include other statistical summaries, but exclude large fitted models,
# plots, functions and intermediate QFeatures objects
additional_objects_68 <- grep(
  "(temporal|interaction|precision|reproducibility|agreement|sigma|residual).*_68$",
  ls(envir = .GlobalEnv),
  value = TRUE,
  ignore.case = TRUE
)

objects_to_save_68 <- unique(c(

  additional_objects_68
))

objects_to_save_68 <- intersect(
  objects_to_save_68,
  ls(envir = .GlobalEnv)
)

objects_to_save_68 <- setdiff(
  objects_to_save_68,
  c(
    "qf_models_68",

    "abundance_precision_68",
    "reproducibility_results_68"
  )
)

saved_68 <- character()
failed_68 <- character()

for (nm in objects_to_save_68) {

  obj <- get(nm, envir = .GlobalEnv, inherits = FALSE)

  if (
    is.function(obj) ||
    is.environment(obj) ||
    inherits(obj, "connection") ||
    inherits(obj, "QFeatures") ||
    inherits(obj, "SummarizedExperiment") ||
    inherits(obj, "ggplot") ||
    inherits(obj, "patchwork")
  ) {
    rm(obj)

  }

  destination <- file.path(

    },

}

manifest_68 <- data.frame(

saveRDS(

gc(verbose = FALSE)

```
Abundance-dependent precision was evaluated across 7,483 proteins shared by all four DIA pipelines using model residual standard deviations across ten within-pipeline abundance deciles. Following exclusion of Group 4, the overall precision patterns remained consistent with the original 83-run analysis. AlphaDIA and DIA-NN maintained comparatively low residual variability, with median SDs decreasing from 0.207 and 0.211 in the lowest abundance decile to 0.118 and 0.100 in the highest decile, respectively. MaxDIA exhibited consistently higher residual variability across the abundance range (0.437–0.298). Spectronaut showed the strongest abundance dependence, with residual SD decreasing from 0.617 to 0.130, representing a 4.73-fold difference. Its particularly elevated variability among low-abundance proteins persisted despite the earlier correction of intensity values equal to 1. Overall, exclusion of Group 4 did not materially alter the relative precision characteristics of the four pipelines, supporting the robustness of these pipeline-level observations to the sample exclusion.


# Publication-ready multipanel figures

```{r manuscript_export_setup, eval=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

manuscript_dir <- file.path(cache_dir, "manuscript_figures")
plot_backup_dir <- file.path(cache_dir, "manuscript_plot_objects")
results_dir <- file.path(cache_dir, "statistical_results")

dir.create(manuscript_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

get_plot <- function(nm) {
  candidates <- c(
    file.path(plot_backup_dir, paste0(nm, ".rds")),
    file.path(results_dir, paste0(nm, ".rds"))
  )

  for (path in candidates) {
    if (file.exists(path)) {
      obj <- readRDS(path)
      if (inherits(obj, "ggplot") || inherits(obj, "patchwork")) {
        return(obj)
      }
    }
  }

  if (exists(nm, envir = .GlobalEnv, inherits = FALSE)) {
    obj <- get(nm, envir = .GlobalEnv)
    if (inherits(obj, "ggplot") || inherits(obj, "patchwork")) {
      return(obj)
    }
  }

  stop("Plot not found: ", nm)
}

clean_panel <- function(p) {
  p + labs(title = NULL, subtitle = NULL, caption = NULL)
}

export_figure <- function(p, filename, width, height) {
  saveRDS(p, file.path(manuscript_dir, paste0(filename, ".rds")))

  ggsave(
    file.path(manuscript_dir, paste0(filename, ".pdf")),
    plot = p, width = width, height = height,
    units = "in", device = grDevices::cairo_pdf,
    bg = "white"
  )

  ggsave(
    file.path(manuscript_dir, paste0(filename, ".tiff")),
    plot = p, width = width, height = height,
    units = "in", dpi = 600,
    compression = "lzw", bg = "white"
  )

  ggsave(
    file.path(manuscript_dir, paste0(filename, ".png")),
    plot = p, width = width, height = height,
    units = "in", dpi = 300, bg = "white"
  )

  message("Exported: ", filename)
}
```

**Figure 2. Precursor coverage and identification overlap across four DIA proteomics analysis pipelines.** (A) Distribution of unique peptide sequence–charge combinations per protein group identified by AlphaDIA, DIA-NN, Spectronaut, and MaxDIA. Boxplots show the median, interquartile range, and whiskers, with counts displayed on a logarithmic (log10) scale. (B) UpSet plot showing shared and pipeline-specific precursor identifications. Intersection bars indicate the number of unique peptide sequence–charge combinations identified by each pipeline combination, while horizontal bars represent the total number identified by each pipeline. Precursors were harmonized using stripped peptide sequence and charge state; modified forms sharing the same sequence and charge were collapsed into a single identifier. (C) UpSet plot showing shared and pipeline-specific protein-group identifications, using exact protein-group identifier matching. Intersection bars indicate the number of protein groups associated with each pipeline combination, and horizontal bars show the total number identified by each pipeline. Filled dots and connecting lines indicate the pipelines contributing to each intersection. All analyses were based on the same 83-sample dataset.

**Figure 3. Comparison of complete protein- and precursor-level incidence submatrices across four DIA proteomics analysis pipelines.** Binary detection matrices for AlphaDIA, DIA-NN, Spectronaut, and MaxDIA are shown at the **protein level (top row)** and **precursor level (bottom row)** across 83 experimental runs. Rows and columns of the original incidence matrices were rearranged using the NIMAA framework to reveal patterns of detection completeness. Colored regions indicate observed identifications, whereas white regions represent missing identifications; colors distinguish the four analysis pipelines. Shaded rectangles outlined in dark gray indicate the largest complete submatrices identified using the *rectangular element-max* heuristic, with the corresponding numbers of retained proteins or precursors and runs reported above each panel. The x-axis represents arranged proteins or precursors, and the y-axis represents arranged experimental runs. For visualization, the precursor-level incidence matrices were aggregated into consecutive display bins, with each bin classified as observed when at least 50% of its entries were present. All reported submatrix dimensions and rectangle boundaries were calculated from the original, unaggregated incidence matrices. Differences in the size and shape of the complete submatrices illustrate pipeline-dependent trade-offs between identification depth and data completeness.


## Fig 4: NIMAA summary
```{r export_NIMAA_lollipop_nestedness, eval=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

# Restore original figures, including their annotations
pA <- get_plot("NIMAA_precursor_summary_figure")
pB <- get_plot("NIMAA_protein_summary_figure")
pC <- get_plot("NIMAA_nestedness_figure")

# Move labels to two lines in panels A and B
move_labels <- function(p, xpos) {
  for (i in seq_along(p$layers)) {
    if (inherits(p$layers[[i]]$geom, "GeomText")) {

      layer <- p$layers[[i]]

      # Convert existing labels into two lines
      if (!is.null(layer$data) &&
          "label" %in% names(layer$data)) {

        layer$data$label <- sub(
          " \\(",
          "\n(",
          layer$data$label
        )
      }

      layer$aes_params$x <- xpos
      layer$aes_params$hjust <- 0.5
      layer$aes_params$vjust <- 0.5
      layer$aes_params$size <- 4.2
      layer$aes_params$lineheight <- 1.3

      p$layers[[i]] <- layer
    }
  }
  p
}

pA <- move_labels(pA, xpos = 20)
pB <- move_labels(pB, xpos = 50)

# Panel C: move mean ± SD labels farther right
for (i in seq_along(pC$layers)) {

  if (inherits(pC$layers[[i]]$geom, "GeomText")) {

    pC$layers[[i]]$mapping$x <- quote(Mean + SD + 2.0)

    pC$layers[[i]]$aes_params$hjust <- 0
    pC$layers[[i]]$aes_params$vjust <- 0.5
  }
}

pC <- pC +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 50)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 50, 10))
pD <- pD + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 2)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1, 1.5))
# Reduce x-axis ticks without changing data limits
# A and B use percentages on a 0–100 scale
pA <- pA + scale_x_continuous(
  breaks = c(0, 20, 40),
  labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")
)

pB <- pB + scale_x_continuous(
  breaks = c(0, 50, 100),
  labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")
)

# Protein nestedness: existing calculated results
colors <- c(
  "AlphaDIA" = "#0072B2", "DIA-NN" = "#E69F00",
  "Spectronaut" = "#009E73", "MaxDIA" = "#CC79A7"
)

d <- NIMAA_protein_nestedness
d$Software <- factor(d$Software, levels = rev(names(colors)))

pD <- ggplot(
  d,
  aes(Nestedness_temperature, Software, colour = Software)
) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(
      x = 0,
      xend = Nestedness_temperature,
      yend = Software
    ),
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", Nestedness_temperature)),
    hjust = -0.25,
    size = 4.5,
    colour = "black"
  ) +

  ) +

  labs(

  ) +

    axis.ticks = element_line(colour = "black"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 14),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 15, face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_line(
      colour = "grey90",
      linewidth = 0.4
    ),
    legend.position = "none"
  )

# Consistent formatting
fmt <- function(p) p +
  labs(title = NULL, subtitle = NULL, caption = NULL) +

    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 14),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 15, face = "bold"),
```

**Figure 4. NIMAA-based assessment of quantitative matrix completeness and nestedness across four DIA proteomics analysis pipelines.** (A) Precursor-level retention of the original quantitative matrix within the largest complete (missing-value-free) submatrix identified by NIMAA. Labels indicate the percentage of the original matrix retained, the number of precursors and their proportion of the original precursor set, and the number of runs retained out of 83. (B) Protein-level retention within the largest complete submatrix. Labels indicate the percentage of the original protein matrix retained, the number of proteins, and the number of runs retained out of 83. (C) Precursor-level nestedness temperature, calculated across 20 repeated NIMAA evaluations per pipeline. Points represent individual evaluations, with annotations showing the mean ± standard deviation. (D) Protein-level nestedness temperature, calculated once per pipeline, with values indicated beside each point. Lower nestedness temperatures indicate more strongly nested missingness patterns. Colors consistently identify AlphaDIA (blue), DIA-NN (orange), Spectronaut (green), and MaxDIA (pink). All analyses were performed on the same 83-sample dataset.

```{r export_figure_4_precision, eval=FALSE}
print(fig5)
```

**Figure 5. Comparison of sample-level reproducibility, quantitative precision, and intensity distributions across four DIA proteomics analysis pipelines.** (A) Multidimensional scaling (MDS) plots showing the distribution of 68 samples processed with AlphaDIA, DIA-NN, Spectronaut, and MaxDIA, colored by experimental condition. (B) MDS plots of the same samples colored by acquisition batch, illustrating batch-associated clustering patterns across pipelines. (C) Distribution of protein-level residual standard deviations (σ) across pipelines, displayed on a logarithmic (log10) scale. Violin plots represent the distribution of residual variability, with embedded boxplots showing the median and interquartile range. Lower residual standard deviations indicate greater quantitative precision. (D) Median protein-level residual standard deviation across ten protein abundance deciles, calculated from log2-transformed protein abundances. Deciles are ordered from lowest (1) to highest (10) protein abundance. Lower values indicate greater quantitative precision. (E) Pooled precursor-level log2 intensity distributions before filtering and normalization, showing software-dependent differences in intensity distributions. Spectronaut exhibits a pronounced low-intensity population and a sharp peak at log2 intensity = 0, corresponding to intensity values of 1. (F) Pooled precursor-level log2 intensity distributions after filtering and normalization. The sharp Spectronaut peak near zero is substantially reduced, whereas its broader low-intensity population persists, indicating that the distinct distribution is not explained solely by intensity values of 1. (G) Pooled normalized protein-level log2 intensity distributions following MaxLFQ aggregation, illustrating differences in the locations and shapes of protein abundance distributions across pipelines. Density curves in panels E–G represent the relative frequency of observed intensities within each pipeline. Together, these analyses characterize sample clustering, batch-associated variation, abundance-dependent quantitative precision, and software-specific intensity distribution patterns across the four DIA analysis pipelines.

**Figure 5. Comparison of sample-level reproducibility and quantitative precision across four DIA proteomics analysis pipelines.** (A) Multidimensional scaling (MDS) plots showing the distribution of 83 samples processed with AlphaDIA, DIA-NN, Spectronaut, and MaxDIA, colored by experimental condition. (B) MDS plots of the same samples colored by acquisition batch, illustrating batch-associated clustering patterns across pipelines. (C) Distribution of protein-level residual standard deviations (σ) across pipelines, displayed on a logarithmic (log10) scale. Violin plots represent the distribution of residual variability, with embedded boxplots showing the median and interquartile range. Lower residual standard deviations indicate greater quantitative precision. (D) Median protein-level residual standard deviation across ten protein abundance deciles, calculated from log2-transformed protein abundances. Deciles are ordered from lowest (1) to highest (10) protein abundance. Lower values indicate greater quantitative precision. Together, these analyses characterize sample clustering, batch-associated variation, and abundance-dependent quantitative precision across the four DIA analysis pipelines.


## Fig 6: Differential abundance
```{r export_figure_6_da_68, eval=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

# Retrieve existing 68-run plots
p6a <- get_plot("p_da_heatmap_68")
p6b <- get_plot("p_da_upset_6h_68")
p6c <- get_plot("p_abs_logfc_68")
p6d <- get_plot("p_precision_68")

# Improve violin plot readability
violin_theme <- theme(
  axis.text.x = element_text(size = 12),
  axis.text.y = element_text(size = 12),
  axis.title = element_text(size = 14),
  strip.text = element_text(size = 13, face = "bold")
)

p6c <- p6c + violin_theme
p6d <- p6d + violin_theme

# Treat each plot, including the UpSet, as one tagged panel
tag_panel <- function(p, letter) {
  wrap_elements(full = p) +
    labs(tag = letter) +
    theme(
      plot.tag = element_text(size = 22, face = "bold"),
      plot.tag.position = c(0, 1),
      plot.margin = margin(8, 8, 8, 8)
    )
}

# Assemble Figure 6
top <- tag_panel(p6a, "A") | tag_panel(p6b, "B")
bottom <- tag_panel(p6c, "C") | tag_panel(p6d, "D")

fig6_68 <- (
  wrap_elements(full = top) /
  wrap_elements(full = bottom)
) +
  plot_layout(heights = c(1, 0.9))

export_figure(
  fig6_68,
  "Figure_6_Differential_Abundance_68",
  14, 8
)

print(fig6_68)
```
**Figure 6. Differential protein abundance, cross-pipeline agreement, and statistical precision across four DIA proteomics analysis pipelines.** (A) Heatmap showing the number of significantly differentially abundant protein groups identified by AlphaDIA, DIA-NN, Spectronaut, and MaxDIA across 11 experimental contrasts. Cell values indicate the number of significant protein groups, with darker blue representing higher counts. Significance was defined using the Benjamini–Hochberg-adjusted p-value (FDR < 0.05), with statistical models adjusted for acquisition batch. (B) UpSet plot showing the overlap of significantly differentially abundant protein groups for the knockout (KO) versus control (CTRL) comparison following 6 h of cisplatin treatment. Protein groups were matched across pipelines using exact protein-group identifiers. Vertical bars represent exclusive intersections, horizontal bars indicate the total number of significant protein groups per pipeline, and connected filled dots identify contributing pipelines. A total of 57 protein groups were significant in all four pipelines, while 551 additional protein groups were shared by AlphaDIA, DIA-NN, and Spectronaut but not MaxDIA. (C) Distributions of absolute protein log2 fold changes for the same KO versus CTRL cisplatin 6 h contrast, shown separately for all testable proteins and protein groups shared by all four pipelines. (D) Distributions of contrast-specific standard errors and absolute t-statistics for the same contrast, restricted to shared protein groups with finite log2 fold changes, positive finite standard errors, and finite t-statistics across all four pipelines. In panels C and D, violin plots show the distributions, with embedded boxplots indicating the median and interquartile range.

**Figure 8. Cross-pipeline agreement, temporal genotype-dependent cisplatin responses, and within-condition quantitative variability across four DIA proteomics analysis pipelines.** (A) Distribution of protein groups according to the number of pipelines detecting a significant genotype-by-treatment interaction, restricted to 7,460 proteins tested by all four pipelines. Significance was defined using Benjamini–Hochberg-adjusted p-values < 0.05. Among these proteins, 5,488 showed no significant interaction, whereas 1,342, 407, 207, and 16 were significant in one, two, three, or all four pipelines, respectively. (B) Temporal classification of the 16 protein groups with significant joint interaction tests in all four pipelines, based on individual interaction tests at 6 and 24 h. (C) Genotype-dependent cisplatin response effect sizes for these 16 protein groups at 24 h and 6 h, expressed as KO minus CTRL responses on the log2 scale. Gray lines connect corresponding protein groups across pipelines, and the dashed horizontal line indicates zero interaction effect. (D) Within-condition quantitative variability, measured as the standard deviation of log2 protein abundance among biological replicates within the same experimental condition and acquisition batch. Boxplots show the median and interquartile range. All analyses used the 68 retained runs, with acquisition batch included in the statistical models. Because 6 h and 24 h treated samples were acquired in different batches, cross-timepoint comparisons require cautious interpretation.

```{r figure_9_export_data_68, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(openxlsx)

# ============================================================
# Figure 9: Export all underlying numerical data
# ============================================================

  cache_dir, "manuscript_figures"
)

dir.create(
  fig9_data_dir_68,
  recursive = TRUE,
  showWarnings = FALSE
)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Panels A and B: JUN abundance per sample
# ------------------------------------------------------------

fig9_AB_data_68 <- jun_data_fig9_68 |>
  dplyr::select(
    Level, Software, Run, Genotype,
    Treatment, Batch, Abundance,
    dplyr::any_of("N_Precursors")
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(Level, Software, Treatment, Genotype, Run)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Panel C: Treatment-specific JUN log2FC
# ------------------------------------------------------------

fig9_C_data_68 <- jun_specific_fc_68 |>
  dplyr::select(
    Level, Software, Treatment,
    log2FC, Lower, Upper,
    P_value, FDR, Significant, N
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(Level, Treatment, Software)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Panel D: Overall adjusted JUN log2FC
# ------------------------------------------------------------

fig9_D_data_68 <- jun_combined_fc_68 |>
  dplyr::select(
    Level, Software,
    log2FC, Lower, Upper,
    P_value, FDR, Significant, N
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(Level, Software)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Panel E: JUN protein abundance and within-pipeline z-scores
# Reconstruct values from the same existing measurements
# ------------------------------------------------------------

fig9_E_data_68 <- jun_protein_68 |>
  dplyr::inner_join(
    jun_design_68 |>
      dplyr::select(
        Run, Genotype, Treatment, Batch
      ),
    by = "Run"
  ) |>
  dplyr::group_by(Software) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    JUN_zscore = as.numeric(scale(Abundance))
  ) |>
  dplyr::ungroup() |>
  dplyr::arrange(Software, Run)

# Save independent clustering order for each pipeline
fig9_E_cluster_order_68 <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  lapply(seq_along(software_order_68), function(i) {

    sw <- software_order_68[i]

    d <- fig9_E_data_68 |>
      dplyr::filter(Software == sw)

    meta <- jun_design_68 |>
      dplyr::arrange(Run)

    z <- d$JUN_zscore[match(meta$Run, d$Run)]

    # Same clustering input as the original heatmap:
    # non-finite values replaced by zero for clustering only
    cluster_z <- z
    cluster_z[!is.finite(cluster_z)] <- 0

    hc <- stats::hclust(
      stats::dist(matrix(cluster_z, ncol = 1)),
      method = "ward.D2"
    )

    data.frame(
      Software = sw,
      Cluster_position = seq_along(hc$order),
      Run = meta$Run[hc$order]
    )
  })
)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Panel F: ROC coordinates and AUC
# ------------------------------------------------------------

fig9_F_ROC_data_68 <- jun_roc_plot_data_68 |>
  dplyr::select(
    Software, FPR, Sensitivity,

  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(Software, FPR, Sensitivity)

fig9_F_AUC_data_68 <- jun_auc_summary_68 |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(AUC))

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Export all sheets into one Excel workbook
# ------------------------------------------------------------

fig9_data_file_68 <- file.path(

  "Figure_9_JUN_Source_Data_68.xlsx"
)

fig9_wb_68 <- openxlsx::createWorkbook()

fig9_sheets_68 <- list(
  "AB_JUN_Abundance" = fig9_AB_data_68,
  "C_Treatment_log2FC" = fig9_C_data_68,
  "D_Overall_log2FC" = fig9_D_data_68,
  "E_JUN_Zscores" = fig9_E_data_68,
  "E_Cluster_Order" = fig9_E_cluster_order_68,
  "F_ROC_Coordinates" = fig9_F_ROC_data_68,
  "F_AUC" = fig9_F_AUC_data_68
)

for (sheet_name in names(fig9_sheets_68)) {

  openxlsx::addWorksheet(

  )

  openxlsx::writeData(
    fig9_wb_68,

    x = fig9_sheets_68[[sheet_name]],
    withFilter = TRUE
  )

  openxlsx::freezePane(

  )

    fig9_wb_68,
    sheet = sheet_name,
    cols = seq_len(ncol(fig9_sheets_68[[sheet_name]])),
    widths = "auto"
  )
}

openxlsx::saveWorkbook(
  fig9_wb_68,
  fig9_data_file_68,
  overwrite = TRUE
)

cat("Figure 9 source data saved to:\n",
    fig9_data_file_68, "\n")

print(
  data.frame(
    Sheet = names(fig9_sheets_68),

  )
)
```

```{r figure_9_six_panel_layout_68, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
resize_jun_heatmap_68 <- function(gt) {

  layout_names <- gt$layout$name

  # pheatmap gtable rows:
  # col_annotation = annotation strips
  # matrix         = JUN abundance row
  annotation_rows <- which(
    grepl("col_annotation", layout_names)
  )

  matrix_rows <- which(
    layout_names == "matrix"
  )

  if (length(annotation_rows) > 0) {
    idx <- unique(gt$layout$t[annotation_rows])
    gt$heights[idx] <- grid::unit(0.16, "cm")
  }

  if (length(matrix_rows) > 0) {
    idx <- unique(gt$layout$t[matrix_rows])
    gt$heights[idx] <- grid::unit(1.15, "cm")
  }

  gt
}
```

**Figure 9. Cross-pipeline assessment of JUN depletion and genotype discrimination in the 68-run DIA proteomics dataset.**

**(A–B)** Distribution of normalized log2 JUN abundance at the protein (A) and precursor (B) levels across AlphaDIA, DIA-NN, Spectronaut, and MaxDIA. Samples are grouped by genotype (CTRL or JUN KO), with point shapes indicating untreated baseline, 6 h cisplatin, or 24 h cisplatin treatment. Each point represents one biological sample/run. Precursor-level abundance represents the median normalized log2 intensity of quantified JUN precursors within each sample. Boxplots indicate the median and interquartile range, with whiskers extending to 1.5 times the interquartile range.

**(C)** Treatment-specific JUN log2 fold changes (KO − CTRL) for protein- and precursor-level quantification. Estimates were obtained using linear models adjusting for experimental batch where applicable. Tile colors indicate the magnitude of the genotype effect, and numerical labels report the estimated log2 fold changes. Asterisks denote Benjamini–Hochberg-adjusted false discovery rates (FDR) below 0.05 across the 24 comparisons.

**(D)** Overall JUN knockout effects estimated separately for each DIA pipeline and quantification level using linear models including genotype, treatment, and batch. Points represent adjusted KO − CTRL log2 fold changes, and horizontal error bars indicate 95% confidence intervals. Green points denote FDR < 0.05 after Benjamini–Hochberg correction across eight comparisons.

**(E)** Independent hierarchical clustering of JUN protein abundance across samples for each DIA pipeline. Within-pipeline standardized JUN abundances (z-scores) are displayed as heatmaps, with samples clustered using Euclidean distance and Ward's minimum-variance method (Ward.D2). Annotation tracks indicate experimental batch, treatment, and genotype. Missing abundance values are shown in gray and assigned a standardized value of zero for clustering only.

**(F)** Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves evaluating the ability of JUN protein abundance to discriminate JUN KO from CTRL samples. Curves were calculated using the 54 samples with finite JUN protein measurements shared across all four pipelines. Lower JUN abundance was used as the predictor of KO status. Legend values indicate the area under the ROC curve (AUC), ordered from highest to lowest.

JNK inhibitor-treated samples were excluded from all analyses, leaving 56 samples for the abundance and clustering analyses, subject to pipeline-specific missing measurements. ROC comparisons were restricted to the 54 samples quantified by all four pipelines.
